title: Don Quixote, Cervantes
subject: litterature
description: Don Quixote charges at windmills, convinced he is fighting giants. Cervantes invents the modern novel out of generous madness, irony, and metafiction.

hero.hook: A country gentleman reads too many tales of chivalry and rides out to save the world.

blocks.text: Published in **1605** and then **1615**, **Don Quixote** by **Miguel de Cervantes** is often called the first modern novel in the West. **Alonso Quijano**, a minor nobleman from La Mancha, decides he is a knight errant and rides out to fight windmills he takes for giants.

The book is far more than a parody of chivalric romance. It invents a new way of telling a story: characters who change, doubt that never lifts, humor and depth at the same time. Cervantes lays the groundwork for the psychological novel and for fiction that comments on itself.

sections.title: Cervantes: a life of adventure and the birth of the novel

blocks.text: Cervantes led an extraordinary life. He was wounded at the **[[Battle of Lepanto (1571) and Cervantes' captivity]]**, losing the use of his left hand, then spent five years as a captive in **Algiers** after pirates seized his ship. Back in Spain and fairly poor, he published the first part in **1605** to immediate success.

blocks.caption: Miguel de Cervantes, soldier, captive, and inventor of the modern novel

blocks.text: In 1614, another writer published a fake sequel. Furious, Cervantes wrote the real second part in 1615, where his heroes discover they are famous thanks to the first volume.
Cervantes mocks the outdated chivalric romances, but above all he invents **narrative polyphony**: every character has a voice, a point of view, and an irony of his own.

sections.title: The founding pair: the Knight and the Squire

blocks.text: **Don Quixote** and **Sancho Panza** make an immortal duo. One dreams of chivalry and perfect justice. The other thinks about his stomach, his wine, and the island he has been promised to govern. Sancho keeps trying to correct his master, above all when the knight charges at windmills he takes for threatening giants.

blocks.caption: Don Quixote and the windmills: the ideal collides with the real

blocks.text: As the journey goes on, Sancho falls for the knightly dream while Quixote begins to doubt under one humiliation after another. This mutual “quixotization” and “sanchification” turns what began as a farce into a deep meditation on friendship, idealism, and clear sight.

sections.title: Metafiction and the play of realities

blocks.text: Cervantes practices **[[Metafiction and narrative reflexivity]]**: he claims to be translating an Arabic manuscript picked up in a market. The narrator is put in doubt, and so is the reader. In the second part, nobles who have read the book stage elaborate scenes to fool the knight.
The pen is the tongue of the soul; the thoughts it forms are the words it speaks.

Madness is no longer only inside Quixote's head. Society manufactures it too, by manipulating him. Identity becomes a story we tell ourselves and a story others impose on us. Cervantes lays the foundations of the modern psychological novel, centuries before postmodernism.

sections.title: Legacy: from quixotism to a universal inheritance

blocks.text: “Quixotism” names a generous, sometimes naive idealism that survives every failure. **Flaubert**, **Dostoevsky**, and **[[James Joyce]]** all drew on it. The novel accepts ambiguity: no single Truth handed down, but conflicting truths carried by individuals.

Beaten by the **Knight of the White Moon**, Don Quixote recovers his reason and dies as **Alonso Quijano the Good**. A final paradox: reason is what lets us live together, but imagination is what gives an ordinary life a heroic shape.

**Don Quixote** invents the modern novel by playing illusion against reality. Cervantes shows that a person can be mad and clear-sighted at once, and that an ideal changes the world even when it fails.
